_note: Claims checked against the public US law store only, so the score is the same on every machine. True claims paraphrase the cited section and should be accepted. False claims must not be accepted. Tune on dev only.

dev.claim: Financial institutions must report currency transactions of more than $10,000.
A bank must file a SAR within 30 calendar days of first detecting the facts.
A bank must keep a copy of each SAR for five years from the date of filing.
Multiple currency transactions in one business day are treated as one transaction if the institution knows they are by or for any person and total more than $10,000.
A suspicious transaction can require reporting if it involves at least $5,000.
Violating this section can lead to imprisonment for up to 5 years.
Breaking a sum above $10,000 into smaller amounts to evade reporting is structuring.
Covered financial institutions must have written procedures to identify and verify beneficial owners.
A bank does not have to file a SAR for a robbery that is reported to law enforcement.

test.claim: Structuring does not require exceeding $10,000 at one institution on one day.
Deposits made over a weekend count as received on the next business day.
If no suspect was identified, a bank may delay filing a SAR by another 30 calendar days.
Reporting may never be delayed more than 60 calendar days after initial detection.
Aggravated cases can carry up to 10 years in prison.
A cash deposit of more than $10,000 must be reported.
Banks must make SAR supporting documents available to FinCEN on request.
A financial institution includes all of its domestic branch offices for currency reporting.
Beneficial ownership procedures must be included in the anti-money laundering compliance program.
